claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily controlled by grain-boundary-mediated heterogeneous nucleation of 1/6<112> partial dislocations that form stacking faults.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi reduces the stacking-fault energy.
The proposed reduction in stacking-fault energy lowers the partial-dislocation nucleation barrier at particular grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary partial-dislocation nucleation dominates the response of Co-free FeNiCrMn at high strain rates and low temperatures.
High strain rates and low temperatures cause an earlier onset of stress drops in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
High strain rates and low temperatures increase the stacking-fault density in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
At elevated temperatures, thermal activation promotes dynamic recovery in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Elevated temperature softens the high-strain-rate response and moderates the low-temperature stress-drop behavior.
The target initial material is an as-solidified, single-phase Co-free FeNiCrMn solid solution.
Controlled comparison of bicrystals or polycrystals with different grain-boundary characters can test the proposed mechanism.
The proposed test regime spans approximately 300-1000 K and strain rates of 10^7-10^9 s^-1.
Grain boundaries such as Sigma3, Sigma9, and Sigma19 can differ in their efficiency as preferential partial-dislocation nucleation sites.
Stacking faults produced by partial dislocations impede subsequent dislocation motion.
The proposed stacking-fault mechanism raises the strain-hardening rate.
Co-free FeNiCrMn should have a lower critical nucleation strain than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi or a corresponding single crystal.
Co-free FeNiCrMn should have a higher stacking-fault density at the onset of plasticity than the selected baseline.
The response should transition from pronounced stress drops at low temperature and high strain rate to smoother flow at elevated temperature.
A stress drop in a tensile stress-strain curve can correspond to grain-boundary nucleation of a partial dislocation.

The hypothesis is limited to single-phase materials in regimes where grain boundaries are the dominant dislocation sources and may fail in the presence of secondary phases or substantial microstructural inhomogeneity.
